Cortez damselfish Stegastes rectifraenum is a common inhabitant of rocky reefs and coral communities throughout the Gulf of California, where it defends algal gardens with notable aggression. Newly hatched prolarvae emerge from demersal eggs after an incubation period of approximately 6 days [ab = approximately 6 days] at the prevailing water temperature of 23.2 °C [T = 23.2 °C]. At the moment of chorion rupture, each yolk-sac larva possesses a minimal wet body mass of only 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams], a value consistent with the small egg diameter of roughly 1 millimeter typical of pomacentrids. This lecithotrophic stage relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves until mouth opening and retinal differentiation enable the onset of exogenous feeding, at which point the tiny larvae begin to pursue planktonic prey. The combination of a brief embryonic period and diminutive starting mass positions the species toward the fast end of the life-history continuum within the genus Stegastes, although direct comparative data for congeners remain sparse.

By the time individuals attain standard lengths of approximately 5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 5 centimeters], gonadal differentiation is largely complete and the fish are considered to have reached puberty. At this developmental benchmark, the corresponding wet body weight typically falls near 2.4 grams [Wwp = 2.4 grams], a figure derived from length-weight regressions established for local populations in the central Gulf. Reaching this size generally requires several months of sustained feeding on benthic algae and associated invertebrates within a defended territory, and pubertal individuals often exhibit the characteristic color pattern of dark grey flanks with a yellow caudal peduncle. Females that have just attained puberty are capable of spawning, though early clutches tend to be smaller and less frequent than those produced by larger, more experienced breeders. The transition to reproductive maturity thus coincides with a distinct shift in both morphology and behavior, as these sub-adult fish begin to participate in the seasonal spawning aggregations that define the species' reproductive ecology.

At their maximum size, adult Cortez damselfish reach an ultimate standard length of about 13.5 centimeters [Li = about 13.5 centimeters], which corresponds to an ultimate wet body mass of roughly 46.6 grams [Wwi = roughly 46.6 grams] according to the regional length-weight relationship. These values place Stegastes rectifraenum among the medium-bodied members of its genus, notably smaller than the giant damselfish Microspathodon dorsalis but considerably larger than the diminutive Stegastes flavilatus common farther south. Large territorial males frequently attain this asymptotic size, and their size advantage plays a critical role in both mate defense and the monopolization of high-quality algal patches. Individuals approaching this final size exhibit a slowing of somatic growth as surplus energy is increasingly diverted toward gonadal development and the maintenance of breeding territories. The ultimate body dimensions are thus a reflection of both genetic potential and the quality of the resources available during the protracted juvenile and sub-adult growth phase.

Reproductive output in this species has been estimated by extrapolation from the better-studied congener Chromis chromis, and at a stable temperature of 23.2 °C [T = 23.2 °C] the maximum daily reproductive rate is understood to be approximately 200 offspring per day [Ri = approximately 200 offspring per day] once females reach full reproductive maturity. This high fecundity is characteristic of many small-to-medium-sized pomacentrids and reflects the substantial predation pressure experienced by pelagic eggs and larvae in the Gulf of California ecosystem. Spawning occurs in distinct bouts throughout the warm season, with gravid females depositing adhesive egg masses on cleaned rock surfaces within male-guarded nests. The combination of high per-capita output and extended spawning seasons allows local populations to maintain robust recruitment despite episodic environmental perturbations such as El Niño-driven warming events. Sustained field observations at a consistent 23.2 °C [T = 23.2 °C] would be valuable to confirm whether the extrapolated rate from Chromis chromis truly applies to Stegastes rectifraenum under natural conditions.

Longevity records for Stegastes rectifraenum indicate a maximum life span in the wild of approximately 11 years [am = approximately 11 years] when assessed at the same thermal regime of 23.2 °C [T = 23.2 °C], making it a relatively long-lived species among its congeners. This extended life span, equivalent to over 4,000 days from hatching, is consistent with an iteroparous life-history strategy in which reproductive value is spread across multiple breeding seasons. Annual survivorship among territorial adults is thought to be quite high, as the combination of strong site fidelity, aggressive nest defense, and a well-developed chemical alarm system reduces predation risk considerably. The demographic consequences of this long life span are significant: populations can persist through multiple consecutive years of poor recruitment by relying on the reproductive contributions of older, experienced individuals. This longevity, when set against the short incubation period of just 6 days [ab = just 6 days], illustrates a classic trade-off between early life history speed and adult persistence that characterizes many damselfishes of the eastern Pacific at a temperature of 23.2 °C [T = 23.2 °C].
